chapter_theme: Neelakesi, having converted Arkkachandra, flies to Padumapuram and opens the Mokkala debate by mocking the Buddhist monks' outward life (the dyed robe, the begging bowl, bodily cleanness, the crafts of a monastery), arguing that restraint lies in the senses and contemplation needs only food; Mokkalan, proud, disputes her victories, recites the Jain categories and calls them the Jina's own invention, and she answers that the Lord's word is truth.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddhist elder at Padumapuram, named in 266 as the Buddha's first disciple and Arkkachandra's teacher
the robed monks of the Padumapuram vihara

267.reading: Neelakesi tells Arkkachandra not to come with her, goes to Padumapuram along the sky as swift as thought, and reaches a vihara where old sayings and their reasons are written out in full, its ground strewn with flowers and golden sand.
267.nuance: The verse runs on into 268 and has no main verb of its own; the place it describes is named as the பள்ளி only in 268. That the vihara's walls carry written sayings with their reasons (மூதுரையும் காரணமும்) fits a Buddhist house of teaching, but that is a reading of a compressed line.
267.event: Neelakesi leaves Arkkachandra behind and flies through the sky to Padumapuram.

268.reading: Seeing the vihara with its makara-bannered gateway, high walls, rows of carved pillars and images like heaven's, she remarks with pity that this splendour is the wealth that ships crossing the shark-filled sea have brought in.
268.nuance: Her first word is a jibe: the monastery's beauty is bought with sea-trade profit, so the renouncers live off merchants' wealth. அளியள் (pitying) sets her tone before any argument begins. குடிஞை (owl, or a carved ornament) is not certain here.
268.event: Neelakesi sees the vihara at Padumapuram and comments on where its wealth came from.

269.reading: Seeing the robed monks, whose conduct and learning match what is said of them and who are called faultless in great penance, she stands in the vihara courtyard holding a cluster of branches of the arasu tree, one leg bent.
269.nuance: இலிங்கிகள் names the monks by their outward sign (இலிங்கம், the mark of an order), which is the theme of her whole attack. The praise in lines 1 and 2 may be ironic. Standing with a hand on the arasu (bodhi) branch inside a Buddhist courtyard is a challenger's pose, as Kundalakesi planted the naaval branch in 228.
269.event: Neelakesi stands in the courtyard of the vihara, holding a branch of its arasu tree.

270.reading: She asks the monks what good comes of their busy work: stitching cloth, dyeing it in ochre and beating it, perfuming it with incense, handling food, with no leisure even to scratch their heads.
270.nuance: The question turns the monks' care for the robe into a householder's chores; the following verses press the same point. Line 3 (தன்னமு மளித்தாய) is not clear; it may refer to giving out food or to something else in the routine.
270.event: Neelakesi asks the monks what fruit their work on the robe brings.

claims.claim: the labour of sewing, dyeing and perfuming robes yields no fruit for one who has renounced

271.reading: When the monks have no answer and sit with bowed heads, she takes their silence as their reply and turns to Mokkalan, the good elder, saying she will question him properly and he must answer without deceit.
271.event: The monks fall silent before Neelakesi, and she challenges Mokkalan to answer.

272.reading: She asks whether the robe is for release, which would then come without knowledge, or for dignity, in which the wealthy outdo him, and what use covering is; Mokkalan replies that covering has a small use, that the form may be known.
272.nuance: Her dilemma leaves the robe only two possible ends, release or prestige, and Mokkalan answers with a third, recognition, and concedes the use is small (சிறிது). The next verses attack that answer.
272.event: Neelakesi asks what the robe is for, and Mokkalan answers that it makes the monk known.

claims.claim: if the robe brought release, release would come without knowledge
the robe has a small use: it lets the monk's form be known

273.reading: She answers that robes are easy to make and hard to keep from harm and thieves, and that the garb serves mainly to tell flesh-givers who you are, you whose heart delights in meat.
273.nuance: விடக்கமர்ந்த உள்ளத்தாய் (you whose heart is set on flesh) carries the Jain charge that Buddhist monks accept meat given to them; the Buddhist side would not accept that the robe exists to solicit it. Lines 1, 2 and 4 are compressed, and the last words (தொட்டைந் பூணியோ) are probably corrupt.

claims.claim: the Buddhist monk's garb serves to make him known to those who give flesh, and he desires flesh

274.reading: She says that a man in such a covering who takes gold will be cornered as a cheat with a low man's hardness, that no one faults his own kind, and asks what he saw that made him take this up.
274.nuance: The verse is obscure: போர்வை பூச்செனின் and வெண்கண்டு do not divide with confidence, and the reading given is one possibility. Its drift fits the verses around it, that the garb invites suspicion rather than trust.

275.reading: She tells him that he hides all his limbs calling it penance because his mind is not firm, and builds many enclosures around himself; it is the eyes, looking at women and other things, that stir the mind, so he should guard them.
275.nuance: Behind the charge stands the Jain (Digambara) practice of going unclothed: covering the body is read as a confession of weak control, and restraint is placed in the senses rather than in cloth. The verse does not name nudity. உண்ணன்மை in line 1 is unclear; it may be 'not eating' or a corrupt form.

claims.claim: covering the body is a sign of an unfirm mind; restraint lies in guarding the eyes, which disturb the mind

276.reading: If, as he says, women would be disturbed on seeing him, and his penance would crumble through their nature, then people will not say there is dignity in his mind, and his virtue falls under no head at all.
276.nuance: She turns his excuse for covering (that women would be troubled) back on him: a penance that a woman's look can break is no penance.

claims.claim: penance that can be broken by being seen by women is not firm penance

277.reading: She attacks the begging bowl: slip and it is lost, stumble and the same, it is a costly vessel that brings much labour and harm, it is not fit for right conduct and hinders the meal, and if one does penance without fault, what is the bowl for?
277.nuance: The bowl (மண்டை) is the Buddhist monk's mark of begging. The Jain ascetic of the Digambara rule eats from the hollow of his hands, which is the unstated contrast. Line 2 (வினை பெரிதால் வினைக்கேடாந் தொழில்) may mean much work, or much karma, from the bowl; both fit her charge.

claims.claim: one who does penance without fault has no use for a begging bowl

278.reading: Water makes the skin clean, betel the mouth, the chewing stick the teeth; if cleaning the outside made the mind pure, she says, then courtesans would have purity of dharma in plenty.
278.nuance: The reductio picks the figure most given to bathing and adornment to show that bodily care says nothing of the mind. It answers the monks' care for clean, dyed and perfumed robes in 270.

claims.claim: outer cleanness does not make the mind pure

279.reading: He left home life as a burden and took up penance, she says, yet he splits firewood, gathers pots, boils cloths with dye and beats them; he cooks dye and cooks flowers: was it only cooking rice he gave up?
279.nuance: The joke is in அடுதி (you cook): the monk still keeps a kitchen, only for dye. சவருடைய in line 1 is unclear; it is taken here as 'troublesome'.

claims.claim: a renouncer who keeps the household's labours for his robes has not renounced household life

280.reading: She lists the crafts he has learned in his penance, dyeing, tailoring and others, and says that had he practised so many trades at home he would at least have eaten his fill; of contemplation there is none.
280.nuance: The names of the crafts in lines 1 and 2 (மச்சிகம், கச்சாரம், சண்ணாரம்) are rare and their sense is not sure. ஓர்ப்பு (reflection) in line 4 sets up 281, where the renouncer's duty is said to be contemplation.

281.reading: She says that if the renouncer's duty is to bring contemplation to completion, he needs nothing but food, and asks whether he has nothing else to teach the dead, those yet to come, those now living and those born in heaven.
281.nuance: Line 3 and 4 are hard to construe; one reading is that his teaching for all beings in all times comes down to this robe-work. The first half is clearer: contemplation needs only food to sustain it, not the crafts of 280.

claims.claim: the renouncer's duty is to complete contemplation, and for that he needs nothing but food

282.reading: She asks whether he alone does not know what all eight directions proclaim, that the body lives by food and awareness by the body, and tells him that if penance without wasting away is what matters, he should end his many entanglements by the belly alone.
282.nuance: The chain food, body, awareness is cited as common knowledge, not as a school's doctrine. It concedes that the body must be fed while denying that anything more (the robe's crafts) is needed. பண்டி (belly) and the last line are not certain.

claims.claim: the body exists by food and awareness by the body

283.reading: Hearing the compassionate woman, Mokkalan, swollen with pride in his possessions, the intoxication of petty learning and the esteem of the deluded, considers what she intends so as to frame a reply.
283.nuance: The narrator judges him before he speaks: the three sources of his pride (wealth, petty knowledge, the regard of fools) answer the opening jibe of 268 about the vihara's wealth. ஆங்காரித்து is taken as 'puffed with ahamkara'.
283.event: Mokkalan, proud, weighs Neelakesi's purpose before answering.

284.reading: Since what she held to as refuge was the Arhat's teaching and the clash between them was real, Mokkalan answers in anger that she has come here like Hiranya and met with trouble.
284.nuance: Line 1 (தரணென்று நன்றென்றாடன்றன்மை யுருவென்றாள்) is hard to divide; தரண் may be சரண் (refuge). The comparison with Hiranya, the proud king destroyed for defying a god, is a threat, and one a Buddhist speaker borrows from Vaishnava story.
284.event: Mokkalan, angered, warns Neelakesi that she has come to her ruin like Hiranya.

285.reading: She replies that there are two here already defeated by her, whom he will know when she names them: Kundalakesi, with waist like a drum and long spear-eyes, and Arkkachandra, who once taught that woman dharma.
285.nuance: Arkkachandra is called the one who taught Kundalakesi (அன்னாளுக்கு அறம் உரைத்த), which matches 227, where Kundalakesi names him as her teacher.
285.event: Neelakesi tells Mokkalan she has already defeated Kundalakesi and Arkkachandra.

286.reading: Looking her in the face, Mokkalan says this is a great lie: Kundalakesi defeated everyone of opposing creeds in the world, wandering everywhere under the vow of the naaval branch and giving dharma to others.
286.nuance: சம்புவிரதி names the challenger's vow of the jambu (naaval) branch that Kundalakesi planted in 228. Line 3 has a doubtful form (வென்றாள்மள்) and line 4 is unclear.
286.event: Mokkalan calls Neelakesi's claim a lie and praises Kundalakesi as undefeated.

287.reading: She says that after hearing him list those defeated, beginning with the Vedic brahmins, and name the creed of each, if he can tell rightly how the Arhat's followers were defeated in the first hall, she will surely defeat him.
287.nuance: Who speaks is not marked, and the verse can also be read as Mokkalan's boast; 288 (எனக் கேட்டு) only says that someone heard it. ஆதிகால் ஆவணத்துள் (in the first hall, or at the first time) is unclear.

288.reading: Hearing this, Mokkalan sets out what the Lord worshipped by the Indras taught: dharma, adharma, time, space, the soul, matter, merit, sin, bondage and release.
288.nuance: The list is the Jain categories as the Manimekalai's Jain gives them (27:171-182), here put in a Buddhist's mouth so that he can mock them in 289. காயம் stands for space (ஆகாயம்) and உருவு for matter, both as the line reads them.

claims.claim: the Lord worshipped by the Indras taught dharma, adharma, time, space, soul, matter, merit, sin, bondage and release

289.reading: He spells out what happens in each of these categories and says that the Lord told them as they arose in his own mind, without knowing the things and their workings as they are, like girls building in the sand at play.
289.nuance: The charge is that the Jina's categories are a mental construction, not knowledge of what is; Neelakesi answers it in 290 and 291.

claims.claim: the Jain Lord's categories arose from his own mind and do not match things as they are

290.reading: When Mokkalan has said this, she laughs and says he does not know the Lord's nature: if Indra worships sages and goddesses as is fitting, can they be called his masters?
290.nuance: Her answer seems aimed at the epithet he used in 288 (worshipped by the Indras): worship by Indra does not of itself make one supreme, so the Lord's authority rests on his nature, which 291 sets out. The construal of lines 3 and 4 is not certain.
290.event: Neelakesi laughs at Mokkalan and begins her answer.

claims.claim: being worshipped by Indra does not by itself make one the supreme Lord

291.reading: She tells him that, not knowing her Lord's nature and scripture, he has not shown a single fault in them even in thought; since what the Lord taught is the truth, are not the categories and their workings stated before established as without error?
291.nuance: The argument rests on the Lord's nature: his teaching is தத்துவம் (truth itself), so the categories need no further proof once no fault is found. Mokkalan's 289 named no fault, only an origin.

claims.claim: since the Lord's teaching is truth, the categories and their workings stand without error

links.note: Mokkalan says Kundalakesi conquered every rival creed on her naaval-branch vow; in 228 the narrator shows the same Kundalakesi, who planted the naaval branch, beaten with drums and driven out of the city gate.
links.teaches: Mokkalan's praise is refuted by the epic's own earlier scene, so the reader sees him defending a champion the story has already disgraced, and his charge of lying falls back on him.

links.note: Mokkalan says the Jina's categories came from his own mind without knowing things as they are; Neelakesi answers that, since no fault has been shown and the Lord's word is truth, the categories stand.
links.teaches: The debate turns on the source of authority: the Buddhist attacks the categories by their origin in one mind, and the Jain defends them by the teacher's nature, so neither touches the categories themselves.

links.note: Both give the same Jain list, opened with the same epithet (இந்திரர் தொழப்படும் இறைவன் in the Manimekalai, இந்திரர்கள் தொழப்படுவான் here) and framed by the same questions of lord, categories, their workings, bondage and release.
links.teaches: The Jain categories circulated as a fixed formula that both sects' epics quote; the Buddhist epic lets a Jain recite it and moves on, while the Jain epic puts it in a Buddhist's mouth so that its defence can follow.

links.note: The Kural says neither shaving nor matted hair is needed if one avoids what the world condemns; Mokkalan grants the robe only the small use of making the monk known, and Neelakesi asks what such a sign is for.
links.teaches: The Kural's dismissal of ascetic marks becomes a live weapon between sects: the Jain debater uses it against the Buddhist robe, while her own tradition's nakedness is a mark of another kind.

gains.a: Neelakesi's question about the robe is seen to rest on an accepted Tamil maxim that outward marks are not the test of renunciation
gains.b: the couplet's general maxim is shown being turned by one order against another's dress, a use it does not foresee

links.note: The Kural says outer purity (புறந்தூய்மை) comes by water and inner purity by truth; Neelakesi lists water, betel and the tooth-stick and says that if outer cleaning purified the mind, courtesans would be the purest.
links.teaches: The couplet's two-part rule is turned into a reductio: Neelakesi supplies the absurd case that proves outer and inner purity are separate, and aims it at monks who tend their robes.

gains.a: Neelakesi's jibe gains a recognised rule behind it, so the courtesan example reads as proof rather than insult
gains.b: the couplet gains a counter-example that shows why water cannot reach the mind, which it states without argument

links.note: Tirumular keeps the body because without it true knowledge cannot be won; Neelakesi cites as common knowledge that the body lives by food and awareness by the body.
links.teaches: The same chain, food to body to knowledge, serves opposite ends: Tirumular uses it to justify cultivating the body, while Neelakesi uses it to say the renouncer needs food and nothing more.

gains.a: Neelakesi's proverb is shown to be a premise other traditions also build on, not her private argument
gains.b: Tirumular's case for nurturing the body is shown limited by a rival use of the same premise, where it licenses only bare food

links.note: Pattinattar counts the begging bowl (இரந்துண்ணும் ஓடு) among the renouncer's wealth without lack; Neelakesi says the bowl is costly, easily lost and useless to one who does penance without fault.
links.teaches: The begging bowl, emblem of renunciation for the Saiva poet, is for the Jain debater a possession that burdens: whether renunciation keeps even a bowl divides the traditions.

gains.a: Neelakesi's attack on the bowl is seen against a living ideal that prized it, so its edge against Buddhist practice is clearer
gains.b: the Siddhar's praise of poverty is shown to keep a possession that a stricter rule would give up

links.note: Sivavakkiyar mocks the ochre-wearers with matted hair, water-pots and yoga staffs who leave their wives and beg from house to house; Neelakesi mocks the monk who boils and dyes his cloth as though he had only given up cooking rice.
links.teaches: Jain and Siddhar both ridicule the ochre-robed renouncer, but for opposite failings: Sivavakkiyar faults him for abandoning home duties, Neelakesi for carrying them on in the monastery.

gains.a: Neelakesi's joke is seen to belong to a wider Tamil satire of the ochre robe, aimed here at its labour rather than its begging
gains.b: Sivavakkiyar's charge that the renouncer abandons home is set against a charge that he never left it

links.note: The Kural says that one who restrains the five senses as a tortoise draws in its limbs is protected through seven births; Neelakesi says the monk should guard the eyes that stir the mind instead of covering his limbs.
links.teaches: The tortoise image of drawing in the limbs is exactly what Neelakesi denies is restraint when done with cloth: she moves the Kural's withdrawal from the body to the senses, against the robe.

gains.a: her charge gains a standard of restraint the Buddhist side would also grant, so the robe can be judged by it
gains.b: the couplet's figure is shown to need a reading, since hiding the limbs literally is what she calls weakness

new_concepts.gloss: formal debate between religious schools, with challenge, reply and a declared winner; distinct from vaadham (alchemy)
new_concepts.label_source: the sarukkam is named மொக்கல வாதச் சருக்கம்; the verses speak of the reply (மறுமாற்றம், 271; மாற்றம், 283) and of those defeated (வெலப்பட்டார், 285, 287)

source_issues: 282 line 4: the edition's '•' for ஃ was repaired by the tool (பஃறொடர்ப்பா).
291: the stanza is printed in eight half-lines and was joined into four by the tool.
273 line 4 (தொட்டைந் பூணியோ) and 286 line 3 (வென்றாள்மள்) look corrupt.
274, 275 line 1, 280 lines 1-2 and 284 line 1 have rare or doubtful forms whose division is not sure.
287: the speaker is not marked; it may be Neelakesi's challenge or Mokkalan's boast.
